papers.title: Altered IL-23/IL-17A immune axis in Parkinson's disease: An exploratory analysis.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with a multifactorial basis. Immune dysregulation, both in the periphery and the brain, has been suggested to contribute to neurodegeneration in PD. Recent research has suggested a crucial role of T lymphocytes, especially the Th17 lineage, in α-synuclein-mediated neurodegenerative disorders. Whether Th17 cells exhibit pathogenic potential in PD is not adequately known. In this study, the role of cytokines that regulate the commitment, development, pathogenic transformation, and effector function of Th17 cells was examined in patients with PD. METHODS: This case-control study was conducted on 46 patients with PD and an equal number of age and sex-matched healthy controls (HC). The serum levels of five Th17-pathway-related cytokines, such as IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, IL-23, and IL-17A, were measured in all the study participants by Multiplex Suspension Assay. The serum cytokine levels were compared between patients with PD and HC. RESULTS: Serum levels of IL-6 (p < 0.001), IL-23 (p < 0.001), TNF-α (p = 0.027), and IL-17A (p = 0.004) were significantly elevated in patients with PD compared to HC. Importantly, IL-6 levels showed a significant positive correlation with TNF-α, IL-23, and IL-17A levels, while IL-23 levels positively correlated with the levels of IL-17A. INTERPRETATION: The findings suggest elevated levels of inducer, mediator, and effector cytokines of the inflammatory Th17 cells in PD. Furthermore, the significant positive correlation between IL-23 and IL-17A suggests an activated IL-23/IL-17A immune axis in PD.

papers.title: Teamwork in Parkinson's care: Building multidisciplinary models worldwide.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a complex, progressive neurodegenerative disorder requiring comprehensive, long-term management. PD affects millions of people globally and presents with motor and non-motor symptoms that progressively impair function and quality of life. While pharmacological therapy remains effective, optimal care extends beyond medication management. Traditional care models for PD often rely heavily on doctors and primarily target motor symptoms and motor complications, with less attention to non-motor symptoms, many of which remain under-recognized. This imbalance contributes to fragmented care and unmet patient needs. These challenges highlight the need for a multidisciplinary care team to address the full spectrum of patient needs. Therefore, integrating a multidisciplinary approach is essential for comprehensive PD management. This manuscript proposes a scalable, multidisciplinary care team model designed to optimise clinical outcomes, enhance quality of life, and remain adaptable across diverse healthcare systems worldwide. It addresses global challenges associated with MDT implementation and outlines potential future solutions. The manuscript also highlights stakeholder engagement in Community Engagement and Involvement (CEI), including initiatives in Tanzania and Thailand to raise community awareness. In particular, the "CheckPD" project and integrated "eat, move, sleep" lifestyle interventions promote lifestyle-based strategies for PD prevention and improved long-term management of PD. Overall, the model emphasises coordinated, patient-centred care that integrates medical, rehabilitative, psychological, and social support services.

papers.title: Outcomes of isolated hip fractures in people with Parkinson's disease: An observational cohort study using propensity score methods.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPeople with Parkinson's disease (PwP) have a high risk of hip fracture and the outcomes of PwP in Australia with hip fractures are unknown.ObjectiveTo describe the characteristics of PwP who present with a hip fracture and to examine the association between Parkinson's with acute hospital outcomes, mortality and discharge destination.MethodsWe conducted a cohort study of individuals with an isolated proximal femur fracture using the Victorian Orthopaedic Trauma Outcomes Registry (Australia) from 2016 to 2022. Demographic characteristics, comorbidities, fracture types, acute hospital length of stay, discharge destination and 30-day and 12-month mortality data were extracted. Inverse-probability weighting with estimated propensity scores determined the association of Parkinson's with outcomes, using a logistic regression model that included covariates and injury characteristics.ResultsOf 5,553 patients, 208 (4%) had PD, with a mean age of 79.9 years (SD 12.9). After propensity score adjustment, there was no association between Parkinson's and ICU admission (OR 1.89; 95% CI 0.67, 5.34), acute length of stay (adjusted median 6.9 vs 7.7) and 12-month mortality rates (OR 1.25; 95% CI 0.85, 1.82). PwP were more likely to be discharged to rehabilitation than home (RR 2.04; 95% CI 1.12, 3.74).ConclusionsWe did not observe a statistically significant difference in acute hospital outcomes between the two cohorts, including length of stay. This is encouraging as avoiding prolonged hospitalisation reduces health care costs and risk of hospital-related harms. However, these findings may reflect limited statistical power and differences between groups cannot be excluded. Further research is also indicated to explore post-care discharge pathways and longer-term functional outcomes of this group.

papers.title: Genetic and personality interactions shape impulse control disorders in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BackgroundIn Parkinson's disease (PD), predictive factors of Impulse Control Disorders (ICDs) remain insufficiently understood. Personality and polygenic risk scores (PRS) have both been independently associated with ICDs.ObjectivesOur objective was to study the interaction effects between personality dimensions and PRS on the odds of developing ICDs.MethodsThis case-control study included PD patients with and without ICDs (n = 250 patients). Personality was assessed using the Temperament and Character Inventory-Revised, and PRS were computed from genotyping data across 18 traits linked to psychiatric/behavioral phenotypes. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate main and interaction effects between personality dimensions and PRS on ICD odds.ResultsHigher scores in Self-Directedness, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-PRS, and major depressive disorder (MDD)-PRS were associated with increased odds of ICD (odds ratios (ORs) between 1.31 and 1.54). Several personality*PRS interactions also significantly modulated the odds of developing ICDs. Notably, Novelty Seeking*MDD PRS and Harm Avoidance*MDD PRS interactions amplified the odds of ICD (ORs = 1.34 and 1.30, respectively), while the Harm Avoidance*ADHD PRS interaction attenuated it (OR = 0.74). Self-Directedness interactions showed both odds amplification (with PD-PRS [OR = 1.34] and MDD-PRS [OR = 1.43]) and slight attenuation (with ADHD-PRS [OR = 0.73]).ConclusionsThis study provides novel evidence that the odds of having ICD are modulated by cumulative and interactive effects of personality and genes in PD. Self-Directedness, ADHD and MDD PRS were individually associated with ICDs, and their combinations yielded complex, non-additive effects-either amplifying or attenuating odds. These findings highlight the importance of integrating both psychological and genetic profiles in personalized risk assessment for I

papers.title: Ambulatory Episodic Hypertension in Parkinson's Disease With Orthostatic Hypotension.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: The objective of this study was to determine whether ambulatory hypertensive episodes are associated with clinical outcomes in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) with neurogenic versus non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. METHODS: Consecutive patients with PD with suspected orthostatic hypotension (OH) underwent 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in the home setting. The primary exposure was the number of hypertensive episodes across 24 hours. Neurogenic OH was defined by a heart rate response to orthostatic systolic blood pressure reduction of <0.5 beats/min/mmHg during standardized 3-minute orthostatic testing. The primary outcome was quality of life measured by the Parkinson's Disease Questionnaire-39 Summary Index (PDQ-39 SI). Secondary outcomes included orthostatic symptom burden and motor severity. Multivariable linear regression models with interaction terms were adjusted for age, sex, disease duration, and levodopa equivalent daily dose, with robustness assessed through multiple sensitivity analyses. RESULTS: Fifty-nine patients with PD were included, 30 with neurogenic OH and 29 with non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension. Among patients with neurogenic OH, a greater number of hypertensive episodes was associated with better quality of life, lower orthostatic symptom burden, and lower motor impairment scores. In patients with non-neurogenic OH, these associations were absent or occurred in the opposite direction. Associations were stronger during daytime than night-time periods and remained consistent in sensitivity analyses. INTERPRETATION: In patients with PD and neurogenic OH, ambulatory hypertensive episodes were associated with better clinical outcomes, an association not observed in patients with non-neurogenic OH. ANN NEUROL 2026.

papers.title: TMEM106B risk converges on C-terminal fragment homeostasis: genetics, mechanisms and therapy.
papers.abstract: TMEM106B is a genetic modifier influencing susceptibility to multiple neurodegenerative disorders, including frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP), Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy, as well as contributing to healthy brain aging and neuronal reserve. The gene harbours single nucleotide polymorphisms and structural variants that define risk and protective haplotypes, and despite extensive efforts to identify the functional variant within these haplotypes, consensus remains elusive. In this review, we synthesize current knowledge of TMEM106B genetics from human cohorts and mechanistic studies, highlighting how variants may influence its regulatory network and protein levels, with an emphasis on its aggregation-prone C-terminal domain. We further integrate evidence on the roles of TMEM106B within the endo-lysosomal system and beyond, including insights into protein structure, posttranslational modifications, interactors, proteolytic processing, and fibril formation. These findings are contextualized using data from mouse and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) models, highlighting current gaps in the available models and the advances required to study its functions and cleavage. Finally, we explore therapeutic strategies targeting TMEM106B, focusing on modulation of expression, specific functional pathways, and fibril formation.

papers.title: Polysomnographic and nocturnal heart rate correlates of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To investigate the correlations between cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease (PD) and nocturnal video-polysomnography (vPSG) and electrocardiogram (ECG) parameters, evaluating their independent clinical value. METHODS: We analyzed 84 PD patients divided into normal cognition (PD-NC, n RESULTS: As cognitive impairment progressed, REM sleep latency significantly shortened (128.82 ± 117.32 min in PDD vs. 200.54 ± 90.26 min in PD-NC, p CONCLUSION: Higher mean nocturnal heart rate and shorter REM sleep latency were independently associated with lower global cognitive performance in PD patients. Both measures can be obtained from routine overnight PSG, although their physiological significance remains uncertain. The cross-sectional design and the absence of direct autonomic or cholinergic measurements preclude causal or mechanistic conclusions.

papers.title: Locus coeruleus abnormalities on neuromelanin-sensitive MRI in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) enables in vivo assessment of locus coeruleus (LC) integrity, but findings in Parkinson's disease (PD) vary across cohorts and methods. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus from inception to 5 September 2026 and pooled independent PD-healthy control (HC) comparisons using random-effects models. Sixty-five reports were included, of which 17 contributed to at least one main pooled outcome. The primary LC-signal analysis included 14 independent cohorts (1,078 participants with PD and 543 HCs) and showed lower LC signal in PD (Hedges' g = - 0.95, 95% confidence interval (CI) - 1.32 to - 0.57; P = 0.00011). papers.title: Parkinson's at the brain border.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease is increasingly recognized as a disorder that extends beyond neurons. In this issue of JEM, Stevenson et al. (https://doi.org/10.1084/jem.20251245) highlight the functional consequence of α-synuclein aggregates at the brain border, uncovering their active role in reshaping lymphatic integrity and the neuroimmune macroenvironment.

papers.title: Binding without Docking: Small-Molecule Binding Paths on Disordered Proteins.
papers.journal: Journal of the American Chemical Society
papers.abstract: Disordered proteins are challenging targets for drug design because they lack well-defined binding pockets. Small molecules can bind them, but when the bound state remains conformationally heterogeneous, these interactions are not readily characterized in terms of conventional binding pockets. Here, we use the concept of binding paths to describe how small molecules interact with disordered proteins. A binding path is a stochastic sequence of transient residue clusters that a ligand engages as it diffuses across a disordered protein, with each cluster forming and breaking up on time scales comparable to the overall residence time. We formalize this approach using a Markov state model (MSM), in which each state corresponds to a set of residues simultaneously contacting the ligand and the transition probabilities capture how the ligand moves between these sets. We apply this framework to the interactions of 10074-G5 with Aβ42 and of fasudil with α-synuclein, two disordered proteins associated with Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, respectively. The MSM enables both a dynamic mapping of transient binding sites and a calculation of dissociation constants consistent with experimental measurements. By generalizing the concept of static binding pockets to dynamic binding paths, this approach provides a quantitative framework for characterizing small-molecule binding by disordered proteins and for identifying druggable regions on these challenging targets.

papers.title: Intelligent exogenous predictive networks for nonlinear Parkinson's disease model involving delay with effects of immunotherapy.
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is used to simulate, solve, or approximate the dynamics of complex neurodegenerative diseases through accurate prediction. Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive disorder caused by the loss of dopaminergic neurons, leading to motor impairments such as muscle stiffness, tremors, and Bradykinesia. In this study, artificial intelligence-driven nonlinear autoregressive exogenous neural networks (AI-NARX-NN) are applied to the existing mathematical model reflecting the dynamics of innate as well as adaptive immune responses to PD under immunotherapy (IAIR-PDI). The IAIR-PDI model is characterized by a delay differential system of five classes representing the densities of healthy neurons, affected neurons, extracellular alpha-syn, activated microglia, and activated T cells. The performance of the AI-NARX-NN is investigated in scenarios of active immunization, passive immunization, and no treatment in the IAIR-PDI model. In the active immunization case, short antigenic peptide vaccination is given to the patients that mimics alpha-syn to generate antibodies, whereas in the passive immunization case, antibody vaccination is given directly to PD patients. The simulation results, including mean-square-error-based convergence curves, histograms, error correlation, solution plots, and corresponding absolute errors, confirm strong agreement between the AI-NARX-NN predictions and the reference numerical solutions, supporting the accuracy of the proposed scheme for the IAIR-PDI model with different time delays.

papers.title: Cellular senescence in ageing and neurodegenerative disorders: Molecular mechanisms, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies.
papers.abstract: Cellular senescence has been increasingly associated with neurodegenerative disorders, potentially linking ageing-related cellular impairment with mitochondrial dysfunction, chronic inflammation, and disrupted intercellular signalling. The present study aims to explore the increasing relevance of cellular senescence among key cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, neural progenitor cells, microglia and oligodendrocyte-lineage cells across neurodegenerative ailments such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis. This review discusses the findings of pre-clinical and clinical studies which suggest that senescence-associated features may contribute to neurodegeneration. Further, it provides an overview of the biomarkers used in the identification of senescence in the CNS. Also, the review examines senotherapeutic treatment approaches, highlighting their actions on different CNS cell types and the growing clinical evidence. It also points out the challenges in translating these approaches to clinical application, such as targeting specific cell types and the lack of suitable biomarkers. Collectively, present findings suggest that senescence-associated alterations may contribute to neurodegeneration, although their effects appear to vary across cell types and diseases.

papers.title: Diagnostic performance and methodological heterogeneity of neuromelanin-sensitive MRI in Parkinson's disease: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) diagnosis remains primarily clinical and is often delayed until substantial neurodegeneration has occurred. Neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) assesses the integrity of neuromelanin-rich nuclei affected in PD, the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc) and locus coeruleus (LC), but its diagnostic performance, technical determinants, and translational applicability remain unclear amid heterogeneity. We aimed to quantify diagnostic accuracy, determine whether performance varies across methodological approaches, and contextualise evidence from clinically relevant settings. METHODS: We systematically reviewed NM-MRI diagnostic studies through December 2025. QUADAS-2 assessed risk of bias. Sensitivity and specificity were jointly pooled using a bivariate model, and AUC using random-effects meta-analysis. Subgroup analyses and exploratory meta-regressions assessed methodological heterogeneity; broader clinical evidence was synthesised qualitatively. RESULTS: Thirty-nine studies were included. Across 20 PD-versus-healthy-control (HC) studies (878 PD; 690 HCs), pooled sensitivity was 89.03% (95% CI 86.01-91.45%), specificity 87.02% (95% CI 82.76-90.34%), PLR 6.86, NLR 0.126, and DOR 54.37. Across 32 studies (1411 PD; 1086 HCs), pooled AUC was 0.909 (95% CI 0.884-0.929; I2 CONCLUSION: NM-MRI is a promising non-invasive imaging biomarker for PD, with strong discrimination across diverse methodological approaches. Harmonised acquisition and analysis, externally validated diagnostic thresholds, and prospective multicentre studies in clinically representative populations are needed to support future clinical implementation.

papers.title: Influence of Temperature and Osmolytes on Conformational Dynamics of Alpha Synuclein.
papers.journal: The journal of physical chemistry. B
papers.abstract: Alpha-synuclein (α-syn) is an intrinsically disordered protein (IDP) associated with amyloid formation in neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy. Disease progression is linked to the transition of α-syn from native to misfolded conformations, although the mechanisms underlying this process remain unclear. An effective method for investigating protein dynamics is native mass spectrometry, specifically when coupled with ion mobility-mass spectrometry (IM-MS) to examine differences in the shape and size of various analytes. In this study, variable-temperature electrospray ionization ion mobility-mass spectrometry (vT-ESI-IM-MS) was used to investigate the conformational dynamics of wild-type and A30P α-syn in the presence and absence of five osmolytes trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), urea, guanidine, 1-dodecylguanidine (dodine), and arginine. For both α-syn variants, the abundance of extended conformers increased with temperature in the absence of osmolytes, consistent with temperature-dependent conformational shifts. This study shows osmolytes significantly alter conformational distributions and temperature-dependent responses, with dodine promoting extended conformations and guanidine producing the lowest abundance of extended states. These results demonstrate the utility of vT-ESI-IM-MS for probing IDP dynamics and highlight the influence of osmolytes on IDP conformational behavior.

papers.title: Metal Ions and Protein Aggregation: Unraveling Molecular Interactions and Theranostic Prospects in Proteinopathies.
papers.abstract: Protein aggregation is a pathological process associated with several human diseases termed proteinopathies, including neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, type II diabetes, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and Huntington's disease. In these conditions, specific proteins misfold and accumulate into insoluble aggregates, disrupting normal cellular function and contributing to disease progression. Many studies have investigated the molecular mechanisms that underlie the aggregation pathways, the structure of aggregates, such as oligomeric intermediates and fibrils, and their cellular toxicity. Studies have also investigated the effects of cofactors like metals, lipids, other amyloid proteins, and small molecules. Recent research has increasingly emphasized the critical roles of metal ions such as copper (Cu), zinc (Zn), iron (Fe), and manganese (Mn) in amyloid aggregation and toxicity. Alterations in metal ion transport, binding, or redox activity have been linked to the onset and progression of several amyloid-associated diseases. These metal ions can interact directly with amyloidogenic proteins, influencing their structural conformation, aggregation kinetics, and propensity to form toxic oligomers. This review aims to advance our understanding of how the regulation of metal ions within cells and their dysfunction contribute to the accumulation of harmful proteins, which is a key factor in proteinopathies. By examining the interactions between metal ions and key amyloidogenic proteins─including amyloid-β (Aβ), α-synuclein, tau, superoxide dismutase 1 (SOD1), human islet amyloid polypeptide (hIAPP), and insulin─we highlight both common and unique pathways through which metal ions influence protein aggregation. Additionally, this review explores the impact of metal ions on protein clearance mechanisms, such as autophagy and the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as well as emerging theranos

papers.title: Neurodegeneration in Sub-Saharan Africa: Intersections of Biological Ageing, Genomic Diversity and the Lifetime Exposome.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are emerging as an important consequence of population ageing in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but their scientific relevance extends beyond a projected rise in case numbers. SSA combines exceptional human genomic diversity with marked heterogeneity in vascular and metabolic risk, infection, nutrition, occupational exposures, air pollution, and access to health care. This combination creates an underused setting in which to study why biological ageing produces neurodegeneration in some individuals but relative resilience in others. This review critically synthesises evidence on Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal degeneration, Huntington's disease and related disorders, focusing on the intersection between hallmarks of ageing, disease-specific proteinopathies, ancestry and the lifetime exposome. Age-associated loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, chronic inflammation, neurovascular injury and genomic/epigenomic instability provide a mechanistic scaffold on which genetic susceptibility and cumulative exposures may act. Yet African evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional clinical phenotyping; neuropathology, longitudinal biomarkers, multi-omics and measured environmental exposures remain sparse. Recent African-ancestry Parkinson's disease genomics and emerging plasma biomarker studies demonstrate that ancestry-inclusive molecular neuroscience is feasible and can generate findings not predictable from European-ancestry datasets. The next phase should therefore move beyond documenting underdiagnosis toward longitudinal, biologically anchored cohorts that integrate phenotype, genomics, blood biomarkers, neuroimaging, exposomics, digital measures and health-system outcomes. This review proposes a research framework centred on biological ageing, gene-environment interaction and resilience. Such work would improve the validity of prevention,

papers.title: Corneal Confocal Microscopy (CCM) in Patients With Central Neurodegenerative Disease.
papers.abstract: Corneal confocal microscopy (CCM) is a rapid, non-invasive ophthalmic imaging technique that enables detailed visualization and quantification of small corneal nerve fibres. Although initially developed for the assessment of diabetic neuropathy, its application has broadened substantially, with increasing evidence supporting its value in a range of central neurodegenerative diseases. This narrative review synthesizes current findings on the use of CCM in dementia, multiple sclerosis, stroke, burning mouth syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, trigeminal neuralgia, migraine and Parkinson's disease. Across these conditions, CCM consistently identifies measurable alterations in corneal nerve fibre density, length, branching and morphology, as well as changes in corneal immune cell populations. These structural abnormalities frequently correlate with disease severity, functional decline and clinical progression. In some disorders, CCM demonstrates diagnostic performance comparable to or exceeding existing biomarkers, and offers distinct advantages as a non-invasive, repeatable and objective measure that can detect early or subclinical neurodegeneration. Corneal confocal microscopy also shows potential as a prognostic and monitoring tool, particularly in conditions with limited reliable biomarkers. It may help stratify risk, track therapeutic response, and provide surrogate endpoints for clinical trials. Despite these strengths, several limitations remain, including modest sample sizes in some studies, variability in image interpretation, and difficulties differentiating between neurodegenerative conditions with overlapping patterns of nerve loss. Emerging automated analysis methods and artificial intelligence-based algorithms may help address these challenges by improving accuracy, reproducibility, and scalability. Overall, CCM represents a promising technique that bridges ophthalmology and neurology. A growing body of literature supports its utility across multiple

papers.title: Acoustofluidic enrichment of small extracellular vesicles: physical principles, microfluidic implementations, and prospects for Parkinson's disease liquid biopsy.
papers.abstract: Reliable blood-based small extracellular vesicle (sEV) analysis for Parkinson's disease (PD) is constrained by co-isolation of lipoproteins and proteins from plasma. This review examines acoustofluidics as a sample-preprocessing and integration-enabling strategy for PD liquid biopsy. We first summarize the analytical value and limitations of sEV-associated α-synuclein, microRNA panels, and multi-omics cargo, and then compare conventional and microfluidic enrichment methods with particular attention to lipoprotein co-isolation, recovery, fraction purity, throughput, and compatibility with downstream assays. We further analyze the physical basis of acoustofluidic separation, including particle volume, density, compressibility, and acoustic contrast factor, and assess its potential integration with on-chip lysis, nucleic acid amplification, protein assays, and signal readout. Current evidence suggests that acoustofluidics can provide label-free, noncontact enrichment of sEV-containing fractions while offering a physical separation dimension complementary to size and buoyant density. However, it achieves reduced lipoprotein co-isolation rather than complete removal, yielding sEV-enriched fractions rather than highly pure isolates. Clinical translation will therefore require standardized pre-analytical workflows, explicit reporting of sEV recovery and lipoprotein depletion, demonstration that improved fraction quality enhances biomarker measurement, and prospective multicenter validation. Acoustofluidics should thus be viewed as a promising front-end technology for improving the analytical reliability and integration of PD sEV liquid biopsy rather than as an independent diagnostic method. The critical question remains whether improved sEV enrichment can ultimately translate into more reliable and clinically useful PD biomarker measurements. We use sEV terminology without assuming endosomal origin.

papers.title: Integrative computational analysis of urinary PAH biomarkers and Parkinson's disease-related molecular signatures.
papers.abstract: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are widespread environmental contaminants with potential neurological effects, yet the molecular links between PAH-related internal exposure and Parkinson's disease (PD)-associated biology remain poorly characterized. We developed an integrative computational framework combining population biomonitoring, transcriptomics, machine-learning prioritization, single-nucleus transcriptomics, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Five urinary PAH metabolites representing complementary biomarkers within the same PAH exposure domain were evaluated in 11,512 adults from NHANES 2005-2018 using complex survey-weighted models. Among 107 participants meeting a prescription-based, single-nucleus transcriptomics, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. Five urinary PAH metabolites representing complementary biomarkers within the same PAH exposure domain were evaluated in 11,512 adults from NHANES 2005-2018 using complex survey-weighted models. Among 107 participants meeting a prescription-based antiparkinson medication proxy, 1-hydroxynaphthalene was the only metabolite associated with the outcome after false-discovery-rate correction (OR per doubling, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.05-1.29; P = 0.005; q = 0.027), with similar estimates across sensitivity analyses. At the molecular level, the five-metabolite biomonitoring panel was retained to identify shared or convergent target features across PAH-related internal-exposure markers. Panel decomposition and leave-one-metabolite-out analyses showed that the prioritized candidates were not dependent on any single metabolite. papers.title: α-Synuclein Binding Alkaloids from the Australian Bryozoan Amathia tricornis.
papers.abstract: In this study, we conducted the first chemical investigation of the Australian bryozoan Amathia tricornis, leading to the isolation and characterization of 11 new metabolites, including the bromoindoles tricornamines A-E (1-5), phenethylamine amathamines E-F (6-7), and guanadino-containing phenethylamides tricornamides A-D (8-11), together with three known compounds; amathamides E-F (12-13) and lamourimidazolinium trifluoroacetate (14). We also report the binding affinity of 6, 7, 9 and 10 to the Parkinson's disease implicated protein α-synuclein. This has provided new insight into the structure-activity relationships of brominated phenethylamino metabolites towards this neurodegenerative disease-relevant target. The new natural products expand the chemical diversity reported from Amathia species and further support bryozoans as a promising source of unique compounds.

papers.title: How a Single-Chain Polystyrene Nanoparticle Dictates α-Synuclein Adsorption and Intramolecular β-Sheet Nucleation.
papers.journal: Langmuir : the ACS journal of surfaces and colloids
papers.abstract: A growing number of studies have detected nanoplastics, particularly polystyrene (PS) nanoparticles, in human blood and various critical tissues. Nevertheless, the molecular mechanisms by which their physical size modulates the aggregation of disease-related proteins remain poorly understood. Here, using well-tempered metadynamics simulations, we demonstrate that single-chain PS nanoparticles with a degree of polymerization N collapse into spherical globules in water, following a scaling law of radius of gyration Rg ∼ N1/3, and that their size critically determines the conformational fate of alpha-synuclein (αS), a key protein in Parkinson's disease. Within our single-chain simulation framework, we observe a sensitive size-dependent transition regime around N = 75 to 80 (Rg = 1.14 to 1.16 nm), where PS nanoparticles transition from insufficient surface area to a threshold capable of encapsulating the αS chain. The partially exposed protein chain subsequently folds into stable intramolecular β-sheet domains, representing the initial nucleation step toward amyloid aggregation. Conversely, nanoparticles with N ≥ 80 (Rg ≥ 1.16 nm) present a sufficiently large hydrophobic surface to completely encapsulate αS through dominant hydrophobic and π-π interactions, effectively suppressing the intramolecular β-sheet nucleation. These findings reveal that smaller nanoplastics may inadvertently promote protein misfolding, which may implicitly lower the likelihood of downstream intermolecular aggregation. Our work establishes a quantitative, size-dependent hazard principle for nanoplastic neurotoxicity and provides a molecular foundation for assessing the risk of environmentally derived nanoparticles in synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Prevalence of alpha-synuclein seeding activity in the Olfactory Mucosa following SARS-CoV-2 infection: results from a pilot study.
papers.abstract: Olfactory dysfunction (OD) is a hallmark of SARS-CoV-2-infection where it is believed to result from neuroinflammation induced by viral invasion via the olfactory mucosa (OM). Hyposmia also affects the majority of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) where it is caused by α-synuclein (aSyn) pathology in the olfactory system, and aSyn-seeding-activity can be detected in the OM using aSyn-seeding-amplification-assays (aSyn-SAA). The present pilot study aimed to investigate whether SARS-CoV-2-infection induces local aSyn-misfolding and -aggregation in OM samples using aSyn-SAA. We conducted an observational study including PD patients (n = 51), individuals with a history of documented symptomatic SARS-CoV-2-infection (post-COVID; n = 95), and healthy controls (HC; n = 42). Post-COVID-participants were stratified based on persistent OD (COVID+OD; n = 42) or normal olfaction (COVID-OD; n = 53) using Sniffin'-Sticks-Identification (SSI) and -Discrimination (SSD) tests. OM samples were obtained by ENT specialists and analyzed by aSyn-SAA at the University of Verona. Clinical phenotyping included MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, and the Innsbruck-RBD-Inventory. OM-SAA positivity rates were significantly different between PD and both post-COVID-participants and HCs (80.4% vs 24.2% vs 11.9%; p < 0.001). Within the post-COVID-group, positivity rates were higher in COVID+OD vs COVID-OD (35.7% vs 15.1%; p = 0.030), and COVID+OD differed from HC (p = 0.030), while COVID-OD did not (p = 0.65). Among post-COVID-participants, aSyn-SAA positivity was associated with lower SSI (p = 0.007) and SSD (p < 0.001) scores, but not with MDS-UPDRS, MoCA, or RBD measures. OM-SAA-positivity was enriched among individuals with persistent post-COVID-OD and correlated with olfactory impairment. These findings support the hypothesis that neuroinflammation

papers.title: Recent advances in the management of Lewy body dementia: evaluating progress and future directions.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Lewy body dementia (LBD), encompassing dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) and Parkinson's disease dementia (PDD), is progressive and heterogeneous in clinical presentation and underlying pathobiology. LBD substantially impacts patient function, independence, and quality of life. Current therapies are symptomatic, and disease-modifying therapies are not established. Advances in in vivo AREAS COVERED: This review examines the complex spectrum of LBD, including DLB, PDD, and prodromal states of MCI-LB and PD-MCI. Advances in biomarkers and biological frameworks are considered along with limitations in DLB. Recent pharmacological and non-pharmacological clinical trials are highlighted. The authors offer commentary on the challenges and opportunities for current and future research and care in LBD. EXPERT OPINION: LBD remains a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge. papers.title: Dissociable associations of free-water fraction and DTI-ALPS index with disease manifestation and mutation carrier status in Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Latent Class Trajectory Modeling Identifies Cerebrospinal Fluid Protein Signatures Associated with Motor Progression in Parkinson's Disease: Evidence from the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative Cohort.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Motor progression in Parkinson's disease (PD) is highly heterogeneous, limiting prognosis and the efficiency of clinical trials that require accurate risk stratification. Traditional modeling approaches assume a single average trajectory and fail to capture meaningful divergence, whereas the biological determinants of trajectory-defined subtypes remain unclear. Multivariate proteomic biomarkers may improve early identification of rapid progressors. OBJECTIVES: We aimed to (1) delineate distinct motor progression subtypes in early PD using longitudinal Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) III scores and (2) identify cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) proteomic signatures that discriminate rapid from slow progressors. METHODS: We analyzed 5-year longitudinal data from 396 Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) participants with early PD. Motor progression trajectories were derived using latent class trajectory modeling (LCTM) of repeated MDS-UPDRS III scores. CSF proteomics from 78 Olink samples were used for biomarker discovery, with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-based feature selection followed by multivariable logistic regression. Validation was performed in 184 SOMAscan-profiled samples. RESULTS: LCTM identified distinct motor progression subtypes in early PD. Differential CSF protein expression across these trajectories highlighted candidate markers of rapid decline. A seven-protein signature (CCL27, CXCL9, NEFL, SERPINE1, GH1, TYMP, KLK1) exhibited good discriminative performance for distinguishing rapid from slow progressors (area under the curve [AUC] = 0.908). In an independent cohort, the combined model showed consistent directional effects and achieved the highest accuracy (AUC = 0.796). papers.title: Liquid-liquid phase separation in neurodegenerative diseases: Mechanisms, pathological transitions, and therapeutic opportunities.
papers.abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) provides a biophysical framework for understanding biomolecular organization, yet its pathological relevance in neurodegeneration remains incompletely resolved. In this narrative review, we critically synthesize current evidence on LLPS in Huntington's disease, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, focusing on mutant huntingtin, α-synuclein, amyloid-β, tau, TDP-43, and FUS. We first outline the molecular principles-including intrinsic disorder, multivalent interactions, and environmental sensitivity-that govern their phase behavior. We then examine how dynamic condensates may, under specific cellular contexts, transition toward less reversible oligomeric, gel-like, or solid assemblies, integrating evidence from in vitro, cellular, and in vivo studies. Importantly, current evidence does not support LLPS as a universal or obligatory precursor of pathological aggregation; rather, its biological consequences appear to depend on condensate composition, material properties, subcellular localization, and proteostasis capacity, while direct demonstration of disease-relevant condensates in vivo remains limited. We further discuss whether aberrant LLPS represents a cause, consequence, or context-dependent component of neurodegeneration and highlight emerging strategies that modulate condensate formation, maturation, or clearance while preserving physiological functions. Overall, this review defines both the mechanistic potential and current limitations of the LLPS framework and identifies key questions that must be addressed before pathological phase-state modulation can become a clinically actionable therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: Mitochondrial dysfunction in neurology: biomarkers and clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a shared downstream pathogenic mechanism across a wide spectrum of neurological disorders, ranging from primary mitochondrial diseases to conditions including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, hereditary ataxias and idiopathic inflammatory myopathies. This Review examines the role of mitochondrial biomarkers in improving diagnostic accuracy, patient stratification and monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response. Primary mitochondrial diseases are presented as proof-of-concept models of impaired oxidative phosphorylation, providing a framework for biomarker identification and validation with translational relevance to other neurological diseases. Mitochondrial biomarkers can be broadly categorized into four domains: fluid biomarkers, reflecting metabolic alterations and stress signalling; genetic biomarkers, capturing mitochondrial DNA integrity and dynamics; multi-omics approaches, integrating transcriptomic, proteomic and metabolomic signatures; and imaging biomarkers, enabling in vivo assessment of structural and functional consequences of mitochondrial dysfunction. Across disorders, these biomarkers reveal shared disturbances in bioenergetics, redox homeostasis, mitochondrial genome maintenance and inflammatory signalling. However, clinical implementation remains limited by methodological heterogeneity, biological variability and reduced disease specificity. Integrated, multimodal biomarker strategies, combined with longitudinal validation, will be essential for supporting precision medicine and guiding the development of therapies to target mitochondrial pathways in neurology.

papers.title: Epinephrine-mediated sensitization of thioredoxin 1 enhances chlorpromazine protection against acute hepatotoxicity.
papers.abstract: Acute liver injury (ALI) is characterised by rapid hepatic necrosis and compromised liver functions. Drug-induced ALI, in particular, is associated with glutathione depletion and overproduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These alterations highlight the contribution of the thioredoxin system (Trx/TrxR/NADPH) in preserving hepatic redox homeostasis. Previously, we demonstrated that thioredoxin-1 (Trx1) overexpression exerts protective effects against ischemic heart and peripheral vascular disease. Also, the neuroprotective role of thioredoxin reductase (TrxR1) has been reported in Parkinson's Disease. However, it remains unclear whether epinephrine (EP)-mediated boosting of the thioredoxin system, together with chlorpromazine (CPZ), provides sufficient protection against drug-induced ALI. To investigate this hypothesis, C57BL/6 mice were chronically administered a low dose of EP to enhance the expression of Trx1/TrxR1, followed by ALI induction with N-acetyl-para-aminophenol (APAP) and treatment with a subtoxic dose of CPZ. In parallel, hepatoma cell lines were treated with EP and/or CPZ to monitor the associated subcellular and molecular changes. The results showed that EP enhanced the expression of Trx1, thioredoxin-like protein 1 (TrxL1), and TrxR1 in liver and TrxR1 in hepatoma cell lines. Also, EP attenuated liver injury and enhanced the therapeutic effect of CPZ in ALI mice. A significant improvement in liver biomarkers, resolution of inflammation, attenuated oxidative stress, and restoration of hepatic histological architecture accompanied these observations. Moreover, activation of the thioredoxin system in hepatoma cells was associated with overexpression of β-arrestin1, TrxL1, and cAMP-response element-binding protein (CREB1), mirroring their involvement in Trx-mediated protection. Conclusively, these results addressed the protective role of boosting the cytosolic thioredoxin system in drug-induced ALI.

Design, reporting, and research focus of neurology and psychiatry drug trials (2020-2023): a registry-based meta-epidemiological study using ClinicalTrials.gov and NLP.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Clinical trial registries document trial design, funding, and results reporting, but heterogeneous and unstructured entries limit cross-trial comparison. Consequently, it is unclear how neurology and psychiatry drug trials are designed and reported in practice, hampering comparison of studies, understanding of the available evidence, and planning of future trials. The aim of this study was to quantify trial design features, results reporting practices, and research focus in neurology and psychiatry drug trials using harmonized registry data. METHODS: This is a registry-based observational study of interventional neurology and psychiatry drug trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov between 2000 and 2023. Using natural language processing (NLP) with manual validation, we extracted and harmonized trial information on phase, randomization, masking, sample size, funding source, results reporting, and target diseases and drugs. We also performed content-based clustering and visualization to explore patterns across trials by drug and disease category. We analyzed temporal trends and differences across trial characteristics. RESULTS: We included 18,609 trials. Most were early phase, single-center, and small, typically enrolling 11-50 participants; 60% were completed. Industry funded 36% of trials, with a declining share over time and a corresponding increase in university sponsorship. Ten percent of trials were non-randomized and 38% were open label. Among trials completed after 2007, 50% reported results, with a mean delay of 12 months. The most frequently studied conditions were pain (10%), schizophrenia (8%), depression (8%), and Alzheimer's disease (7%). Drug testing was widely distributed, with atypical antipsychotics, levodopa, and ketamine each accounting for 1-2% of trials. Content-based clustering identified disease-specific groupings of trials. papers.title: Gene-based association analysis of depression risk among European ancestry Parkinson's disease patients.
papers.abstract: Depression is one of the most common and disabling non-motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease (PD), yet its genetic basis remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the genetic contributions to depression in PD by estimating the burden from common as well as low-frequency single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) within genes previously implicated in PD or depression risk among European ancestry PD patients from three population-based studies. Using gene-based association analyses (SKAT, Burden, and SKAT-O) in the PASIDA, PEG, and PPMI studies, we evaluated SNP sets in gene regions previously linked to PD or depression. Among PD-related genes, meta-analysis identified a significant association between KRTCAP2 and self-reported depression diagnosis in PD (SKAT-O p = 4.33 × 10⁻⁵), which remained significant after false discovery rate correction. A higher genetic burden in KRTCAP2 was associated with 20% increased odds of depression (OR = 1.20, 95% CI: 1.04-1.38). TRAF5 and LRRK2 showed marginal associations. Among depression-related genes, SPPL3 and ERBB4 were associated with depression diagnosis history, and FNIP2 was associated with current depressive symptoms. The PD polygenic risk score was not associated with depression in PD, while a higher depression polygenic risk score was significantly associated with increased odds of depression diagnosis in both cohorts and the meta-analysis (OR = 1.26, 95% CI: 1.13-1.40). Our findings highlight immune-related genes such as KRTCAP2 and TRAF5 as potential contributors to depression in PD. Additionally, the depression PRS shows statistically significant association with depression diagnosis in PD, suggesting that a general depression-related genetic liability contributes to this non-motor feature in PD. papers.title: Cell-type dependence of effects from transcranial electric brain stimulation.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent need for better treatment options for many neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, depression, and epilepsy. Transcranial electrical stimulation (tES) is a non-invasive, safe, inexpensive, and promising method that could address some of this unmet need. The therapeutic value of tES has been well demonstrated, but the effect is highly variable. To enable tES to reach its full potential requires a better understanding of how tES modulates neural activity so that tES treatments can be tailored to specific neurological conditions and individual patients. The neural response to tES is, however, highly complex, and the parameter space involved in optimizing tES treatments is daunting. This has made it difficult to obtain general insights into how tES modulates neural activity, and a central challenge lies in the cell-type-specific and frequency-dependent nature of these responses. In this study, we investigated cell-type-specific neuronal responses to tES over a broad frequency range, using a large database of biophysically detailed neuron models. We found that pyramidal cells respond strongly to low-frequency tES, but their responses drop sharply with frequency. In contrast, inhibitory neurons show a smaller reduction and, on average, become more responsive than pyramidal cells above ~60 Hz. By leveraging a reciprocity theorem we demonstrated that the effect of tES on a given cell-type is proportional to the frequency-dependent current-dipole moment that determines the EEG-signal contribution of this cell-type. We further identified the dendritic asymmetry as key in determining tES responses across the frequency spectrum. Counterintuitively, we also found that while total cell length increases tES sensitivity at low frequencies, it can have the opposite effect at high frequencies. papers.title: STN-SNr co-stimulation in Parkinson's disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis of motor and freezing-of-gait outcomes.
papers.journal: Neurological sciences : official journal of the Italian Neurological Society and of the Italian Society of Clinical Neurophysiology
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Freezing of gait (FoG) and axial impairments often persist in Parkinson's disease despite optimized medication and subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS). We systematically reviewed whether adding substantia nigra pars reticulata (SNr) stimulation improves motor and FoG outcomes. METHODS: Following PRISMA 2020 and PROSPERO registration (CRD420261343479), six databases were searched through 1 May 2026. Primary outcomes compared STN-SNr co-stimulation with STN-only stimulation; stimulation-off or baseline comparisons were secondary. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias. UPDRS-III and FoG were pooled as mean differences (MDs) and Hedges' g, respectively, accounting for paired data and within-study dependence. Certainty was assessed using GRADE. RESULTS: Ten studies (nine randomized trials and one observational study) included 109 unique evaluable participants; two single-patient case reports were summarized narratively. UPDRS-III showed no between-group difference across seven studies (73 participants; MD - 0.10, 95% CI - 1.01 to 0.81; I² = 0%; low certainty). FoG showed no additional benefit across six studies (86 participants; Hedges' g - 0.23, 95% CI - 1.04 to 0.59; I²_total = 85.6%; very low certainty). Secondary baseline comparisons favored co-stimulation for UPDRS-III (MD - 13.55) and FoG (Hedges' g - 0.60), but did not isolate an incremental SNr effect. CONCLUSIONS: Low-certainty evidence suggests no clinically important difference in global motor outcomes, while very-low-certainty evidence does not demonstrate a consistent additional FoG benefit. Improvements versus stimulation-off or baseline cannot establish an incremental SNr effect. Larger phenotype-stratified trials with objective gait endpoints and systematic adverse-event reporting are needed.

papers.title: The FOG-COA Protocol: Validation of Freezing of Gait Clinical Outcomes Assessments in Parkinson's Disease.
papers.abstract: The development and evaluation of novel treatment options for freezing of gait (FOG) in Parkinson's disease have been limited by an ambiguous definition and lack of standardized clinical outcome assessments (COAs) that 1) reliably assess FOG severity, 2) are responsive to change, and 3) capture patient-relevant impact. To address these gaps, working groups from the International Consortium on FOG (ICFOG) developed a clinician-rated outcome-the Giladi Protocol for assessing FOG severity (GP-FOG), and a patient-reported outcome-the FOG Quality of Life questionnaire (FOG-QOL). The FOG-COA project will evaluate the conceptual framework and psychometric properties of these COAs to determine their fit-for-purpose in clinical trials. A total of 105 freezers and 35 non-freezers from seven international centers will complete the GP-FOG in the dopaminergic OFF and ON states during two separate visits (7-14 days apart). FOG annotations from video recordings will be used to assess criterion validity. OFF and ON GP-FOG scores from two trained raters at Visit 1, as well as within-rater scores across visits, will examine reliability. Responsiveness will be evaluated by comparing effect sizes between OFF and ON GP-FOG scores. Patient meaningfulness will be assessed through the association between patient-perceived FOG severity and GP-FOG scores. Participants will complete the FOG-QOL at each visit to assess test-retest reliability and validity against the NFOGQ and PDQ-8. A subset of freezers will undergo cognitive interviews to identify relevant daily life FOG impacts and evaluate FOG-QOL meaningfulness. Collectively, this work will advance standardized, sensitive, and meaningful FOG-COAs, supporting regulatory-grade endpoints and the development of a multi-dimensional outcome framework.

papers.title: Beyond motor recovery: subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation may improve blinking and dry eye symptoms without restoring tear film homeostasis in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: PURPOSE: To investigate the longitudinal effects of subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation (STN-DBS) on objective and subjective dry eye parameters in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: This retrospective observational study included 34 patients with advanced PD who underwent STN-DBS. Comprehensive ophthalmic examinations were performed were performed before surgery and at postoperative week 1, month 1, and month 4. Outcome measures included spontaneous blink rate, tear break-up time (TBUT), Schirmer I test, Oxford corneal staining score, and the Ocular Surface Disease Index (OSDI). Longitudinal changes were analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE). RESULTS: Spontaneous blink rate increased significantly over time, reaching statistical significance at postoperative month 4 compared with baseline (rate ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.04-1.36; p = 0.014). OSDI scores showed progressive improvement throughout follow-up, with significantly lower scores at postoperative week 1 (p = 0.038), month 1 (p = 0.036), and month 4 (p = 0.002). In contrast, no significant longitudinal changes were observed in TBUT (p = 0.552), Schirmer I test results (p = 0.992) or Oxford corneal staining scores (p = 0.090). CONCLUSIONS: STN-DBS was associated with increased spontaneous blinking and significant improvement in subjective dry eye symptoms in patients with PD, whereas objective measures of tear film stability, tear production, and ocular surface integrity remained unchanged during short-term follow-up. These findings may suggest that the ocular benefits of STN-DBS may be mediated primarily through modulation of central neural mechanisms governing blink regulation and symptom perception rather than restoration of peripheral tear film homeostasis. Continued ophthalmic evaluation and conventional dry eye management remain important following STN-DBS.

papers.title: Remote Versus In-Person Follow-up Programming After Subthalamic Deep Brain Stimulation for Parkinson's Disease: A Multicenter Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Remote programming of deep brain stimulation may improve access to specialized postoperative care for people with Parkinson's disease, but prospective randomized evidence remains limited. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to determine whether remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation is noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up programming for motor outcomes during the early postoperative period. METHODS: In this prospective, randomized, open-label, multicenter noninferiority trial, adults with idiopathic Parkinson's disease who recently underwent bilateral subthalamic nucleus deep brain stimulation implantation at six German centers were randomly assigned 1:1 to conventional in-person follow-up programming or remote follow-up programming through a secure telemedicine platform during the first 90 days after surgery. All participants underwent initial in-person postoperative programming before randomization. The primary outcome was the Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale Part III score at 90 days in the medication on and stimulation ON state. The prespecified noninferiority margin was 5 points. RESULTS: Fifty-two participants were randomly assigned. The per-protocol population included 26 participants in the conventional care group and 22 in the remote programming group. The between-group median difference of the primary endpoint was -2.5 points (95% confidence interval, -9.0 to 2.0), meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion. Secondary clinical outcomes and patient-reported outcomes were broadly comparable between groups. Serious adverse events occurred at similar frequencies in both groups, and no deaths occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Remote follow-up programming after standardized inpatient initiation achieved motor outcomes noninferior to conventional in-person follow-up during the first 3 months, with no clear short-term safety signal. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Emerging links between gut dysbiosis, aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation, and Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most common progressive neurodegenerative disorder, is classically defined as a motor disorder characterized by dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra and motor dysfunction. Increasing evidence, however, identifies PD as a multisystem disorder with early non-motor features, including sleep, psychiatric, and gastrointestinal disturbances, implicating the gut-brain axis. Tryptophan metabolism through serotonin, kynurenine, and indole pathways generates bioactive metabolites, many of which regulate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR). AhR is a ligand-activated transcription factor involved in xenobiotic metabolism through canonical signaling pathways; however, growing evidence supports its role in immune balance, glial responses, and barrier integrity. Altered AhR signaling may therefore connect gut dysbiosis and disrupted tryptophan metabolism to sustained, systemic and central inflammation in PD. This review examines gut dysbiosis, tryptophan metabolism, and AhR signaling as potential mechanisms underlying idiopathic PD and highlights their relevance to early diagnosis and disease-modifying therapies.

papers.title: Circadian rhythms in health and disease.
papers.abstract: Circadian rhythms, serving as a crucial temporal bridge linking neural activity and pathological biology, are regulated by central pacemaker neurons to maintain cellular homeostasis and coordinate diverse biological processes. Circadian rhythm disruption is closely associated with various diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, metabolic disorders, and cancer. Circadian rhythms are controlled by core clock genes, such as BMAL1 and CLOCK, modulating numerous physiological processes, encompassing metabolism, immune responses, neural activity, and hormone regulation. Circadian rhythms disruptions arising from shift work, jet lag, or inconsistent sleep schedules are implicated in both the onset and progression of numerous diseases, notably Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The article highlights how circadian dysregulation alters cellular processes to potentially accelerate disease progression. Circadian disruption results in impaired immune function, further promoting disease development and resistance to treatment. Potential therapeutic applications based on circadian biology, such as chronotherapy and personalized medicine, are also discussed. Recent technological advances, embodied in wearable devices and omics approaches, are increasingly providing deeper insights into circadian biology. Further unveiling the role of circadian in health and disease opens new avenues for tailoring treatment timing to patients' biological rhythms, thereby enhancing therapeutic outcomes across various diseases. By bridging fundamental circadian mechanisms with clinical pathology, this review provides a roadmap for future chronotherapeutic interventions in precision medicine.

papers.title: Astaxanthin alleviates Parkinson's disease via dual regulation of tryptophan metabolism: central STAT3/IDO1 inhibition and gut microbiota remodeling.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with limited disease-modifying treatments. Dysregulation of tryptophan metabolism via the gut-brain axis has emerged as a key pathogenic mechanism. Astaxanthin (AX), a dietary ketocarotenoid abundant in Haematococcus pluvialis and marine organisms, possesses potent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties; however, it remains unclear whether AX exerts neuroprotection in PD through specific modulation of tryptophan metabolism via the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3)/ indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1 (IDO1) pathway and gut microbiota remodeling. In this study, an MPTP (1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine) induced mouse model of PD was used to evaluate the neuroprotective effects of AX. AX ameliorated motor deficits, attenuated dopaminergic neuron loss in the substantia nigra (SN), suppressed neuroinflammation, and enhanced mitophagy. Mechanistically, AX directly inhibited STAT3 activation and downregulated IDO1 expression in the brain, reducing the conversion of tryptophan to neurotoxic quinolinic acid (QUIN). Concurrently, AX reshaped the gut microbiota by enriching Lactobacillus, which redirected tryptophan metabolism toward the production of neuroprotective indole derivatives, including indole-3-propionic acid (IPA) and indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from AX-treated donors recapitulated key aspects of these effects, including suppression of signal transducer and activator of transcription 3(STAT3)/ indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1(IDO1), elevation of IPA/IAA, and improvement of motor function, confirming that the gut microbiota mediates AX's neuroprotective action. These findings demonstrate that AX alleviates PD pathology through a dual mechanism: central inhibition of the STAT3/IDO1 pathway to block neurotoxic quinolinic acid production, and peripheral gut microbiota remodeling to enhance neuroprotective indole derivatives. papers.title: Habitual Diet, Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis, and α-Synucleinopathy Conversion in Isolated Rapid Eye Movement (REM) Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Accumulating evidence indicates that habitual diet, including plant-based dietary patterns, is associated with neurodegenerative α-synucleinopathy risk. However, the role of diet and its correlation with the gut microbiome in prodromal α-synucleinopathy, specifically among patients with isolated rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (iRBD), remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate dietary patterns, their interplay with gut microbial dysbiosis, and longitudinal effects on neurodegenerative progression in iRBD patients. METHODS: We recruited 287 iRBD patients and 208 age- and sex-matched controls. Plant-based diet indices (PDIs) were derived from food frequency questionnaires. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed in 456 subjects for diet-microbiome analyses. After a median follow-up of 4.2 years, 45 (15.7%) iRBD patients converted to α-synucleinopathies. Cox proportional hazards models assessed the associations between diet and neurodegenerative outcomes. RESULTS: We found that iRBD patients exhibited lower healthful PDIs (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 95% confidence interval [95% CI]: 0.48 [0.29-0.80], P = 0.005) but higher consumption of unhealthful plant-based foods (refined grains, sweets, and sweeteners). Diet-microbiome interaction analysis identified dietary associations for 84.3% of iRBD-related gut microbes, including co-occurrence between healthful PDI and Clostridium sp. AF20-17LB. Longitudinally, four dietary factors and five iRBD-related microbes were associated with neurodegenerative outcomes; specifically, higher coffee consumption was linked to a lower risk of progression to α-synucleinopathy (aHR [95% CI]: 0.30 [0.11-0.78], P = 0.01). Furthermore, mediation analyses indicated that the iRBD-enriched species Ruthenibacterium lactatiformans mediated the association between unhealthful PDI and dementia-first conversion. CONCLUSIONS: Habitual diet in iRBD is associated wit

papers.title: Dysarthria and idiopathic Parkinson's disease: a current overview of the relationship between speech impairment and quality of life.
papers.abstract: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease (IPD) is a chronic and progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, and impairment of automatic movements. Dysarthria is one of the most common manifestations, significantly impacting communication and quality of life (QoL). The Living with Dysarthria (LwD) questionnaire is a tool developed to assess the functional and psychosocial impact of this condition, providing a patient-centered measure of symptom severity. This article aims to present a literature review on the impact of dysarthria in IPD and the use of the LwD questionnaire in evaluating patients' QoL. Five studies investigating dysarthria in IPD and its impact on QoL using the LwD were selected, with searches conducted in the SciELO and PubMed databases, including one study presented at a conference in 2024. The analyzed studies showed that dysarthria compromises not only speech but also emotional and social aspects, directly affecting self-esteem and social participation. The evidence reinforces the importance of integrated therapeutic approaches that address both motor and psychosocial limitations of communication. Furthermore, there is a need for new studies using the LwD specifically in IPD patients to strengthen the scientific basis and improve intervention and therapeutic strategies.

papers.title: The role of polysomnography in Parkinson's disease: objective sleep assessment and clinical indications.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders (SDs) are highly prevalent in Parkinson's disease (PD), affecting up to 80% of patients during the disease and significantly contributing to impaired quality of life, cognitive decline, motor worsening, fall risk, and increased caregiver burden. Polysomnography (PSG) remains the gold standard for objective sleep assessment in PD and plays a central role in differential diagnosis and therapeutic planning. This review examines the spectrum of SDs identifiable by PSG, including rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), periodic limb movements in sleep, and alterations in sleep architecture. Video-polysomnography (v-PSG) is essential for confirming REM sleep without atonia (RWA), which is the electrophysiological hallmark of RBD and a recognized prodromal marker of synucleinopathies. Also, PSG quantifies the apnea-hypopnea index (AHI), oxygen desaturation burden, and sleep fragmentation, parameters associated with cognitive impairment and disease progression. While home sleep apnea testing (HSAT, type 3) may be useful for selected cases with high suspicion of OSA, comprehensive in-laboratory (type 1) PSG provides superior diagnostic accuracy, particularly in patients with complex or overlapping sleep disturbances. Integrating objective sleep evaluation into routine PD management is crucial to identify treatable comorbidities, improve prognostic stratification, and optimize motor and non-motor outcomes.

papers.title: Drosophila Models of Human Neurodegenerative Diseases.
papers.abstract: In his book Insects and the Life of Man: Collected Essays on Pure Science and Applied Biology, Sir V. B. Wigglesworth examined how a fundamental understanding of insect physiology and biology can be applied to some of society's greatest challenges, including human health. Here we reflect on how, in the 50 years since his book's publication, Drosophila melanogaster have played a critical role in advancing our understanding of human neurodegenerative diseases. Focusing on Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, and the frontotemporal dementia / amyotrophic lateral sclerosis spectrum, we examine the role Drosophila have played in elucidating fundamental mechanisms of neurodegeneration, identifying therapeutic targets, and dissecting the complex interplay that exists between genetics and environmental factors. Together these studies highlight how Drosophila models continue to provide critical insight into the molecular mechanisms underpinning neurodegeneration and provide a fundamental pre-clinical model in which we can accelerate research into human neurodegenerative conditions.
